stimuli.title: Clinton's Ditch: How the Erie Canal Changed a Nation
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] In the early 1800s, the Appalachian Mountains stood like a wall between the cities of the East Coast and the fast-growing farms of the Great Lakes region and the Ohio Valley. Moving goods across that wall was slow and expensive. A wagon hauling flour over rough mountain roads could take weeks to reach the coast, and the cost of the trip often ate up most of a farmer's profit. Many western farmers found it cheaper to float their crops down the Mississippi River to New Orleans than to send them east. To leaders in New York, this was both a problem and an opportunity.

[2] The idea of a canal across upstate New York, linking the Hudson River to Lake Erie, had been discussed for years. In 1809, supporters asked the federal government to help pay for it. President Thomas Jefferson reportedly dismissed the plan as “little short of madness.” At the time, the longest canal in the United States ran only about 27 miles. The proposed canal would run about 363 miles, through forests, swamps, and rocky ridges. Turned down by Washington, New York decided to build the canal on its own. DeWitt Clinton, who became governor in 1817, was its loudest champion. His opponents were just as loud, mocking the project as “Clinton's Ditch” and warning that it would bankrupt the state.

[3] Construction began on July 4, 1817, in the town of Rome, New York. Crews cleared trees, pulled stumps, and dug the channel largely by hand, with shovels, picks, and teams of horses and mules. The finished canal was 40 feet wide and only 4 feet deep. Thousands of laborers did the work, among them local farmers and newly arrived immigrants, many from Ireland. None of the project's chief engineers had formal engineering training; most had worked as land surveyors, and they learned much of their craft on the job. One of them, Canvass White, developed a cement that hardened underwater, which allowed builders to make stone locks that would last.

[4] Changes in elevation were the canal's greatest challenge. Lake Erie sits about 570 feet higher than the Hudson River at Albany, and boats cannot float uphill. The builders solved the problem with 83 locks. A lock works like a water elevator: a boat enters a stone chamber, gates close behind it, and water is let in or drained out until the boat rises or falls to the next level. At Lockport, near the western end, engineers built a staircase of five paired locks to lift boats up a steep rock ridge called the Niagara Escarpment. Visitors came from far away just to watch.

[5] The canal opened in October 1825. To celebrate, Governor Clinton traveled by boat from Buffalo to New York City, where he poured a keg of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean in a ceremony called the “Wedding of the Waters.” The results soon silenced most critics. The cost of shipping a ton of goods between Buffalo and New York City fell from about $100 to about $10, and goods moved far faster than they ever had by wagon. Tolls collected from canal boats repaid the state's roughly $7 million construction cost within about ten years. New York City became the busiest port in the nation, and towns along the route, such as Syracuse, Rochester, and Buffalo, grew into cities. Thousands of settlers rode the canal west to Ohio, Michigan, and beyond.

[6] Not everyone gained. The flood of settlers sped the loss of land by Native nations, including the Haudenosaunee, whose homelands the canal crossed. Within a few decades, railroads began to carry much of the freight that canal boats once had. Still, the Erie Canal proved that a bold public project, doubted by many, could reshape the economy of an entire region. Today, a modern, enlarged version of the canal still carries boats across the state, and cyclists ride trails along much of the original route.

Our records show that your order left our warehouse on schedule. Unfortunately, a winter storm delayed the delivery truck, and the box was damaged when it (2) from one truck to another at our regional center. That explanation does not excuse the problem. The quality of our furniture and the satisfaction of our customers (3) our top priorities, and we fell short of both.

We have already shipped a replacement table (4) should arrive by Friday, March 14. Packed in a reinforced wooden crate, (5). The driver will take the damaged table away when he delivers the new one. (6), you do not need to repack it or return it yourself.

stimuli.title: The Unfinished Chair
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] The workshop behind Grandpa Elias's house smelled the way it always had, of cedar shavings and machine oil and the coffee he used to forget on the windowsill. Theo had not been inside since the funeral in March. Now it was June, and his mother had asked him to clear the place out before the house went on the market.

[2] He meant to work quickly. He had brought a roll of trash bags and one cardboard box for anything worth selling. But the first thing he saw when he switched on the light was the rocking chair, standing in the middle of the floor like a guest who had arrived too early. Its seat was smooth, and its back was carved with a pattern of oak leaves, but it had only one rocker. The second lay across the workbench, roughly shaped, with pencil marks still on it.

[3] Theo remembered the summer he was twelve, when his grandfather had tried to teach him to use a hand plane. Theo had pushed too hard, and the blade dug in and tore a gash in the board. “Don't fight the wood,” Grandpa Elias had said, laying his own hand over Theo's. “Read the grain. It will tell you which way it wants to go.” Theo had rolled his eyes and gone back inside to play video games. He had not picked up a tool since.

[4] Now he ran his thumb along the unfinished rocker. Under the pencil marks, in his grandfather's cramped handwriting, were two words: For Theo.

[5] He sat down on an overturned bucket. For a long time, he did not move. Outside, a neighbor's lawn mower droned and stopped and droned again.

[6] Then he stood, found the hand plane hanging in its place on the pegboard, and tested the blade with his thumb the way he had seen his grandfather do a hundred times. It was sharp. Of course it was.

[7] His first stroke skipped and chattered across the wood. His second tore a small chip from the edge, and he muttered under his breath. He set the plane down and studied the board, following the fine lines that ran through it like currents in a slow river, and then he turned it around. This time, the blade slid forward, and a thin, curling ribbon of cedar rose from it and dropped to the floor.

[8] Theo worked until the light through the window turned orange. He did not finish the rocker that day, or the next. His mother called twice to ask how the clearing out was going. “Slowly,” he told her, which was true.

[9] By the end of the week, the trash bags were still folded on the workbench, and the floor around the chair was covered in pale curls of wood.

stimuli.title: Lock the Phones Away and Let Students Learn
stimuli.source: By Dr. Angela Ruiz, principal of Lakeview High School. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Walk into almost any high school classroom today and you will see the same thing: students glancing at screens hidden under their desks, thumbs moving while a teacher explains a math problem. Phones were designed to capture attention, and they are very good at it. That is exactly why high schools should ban student cell phones from the first bell to the last.

At Lakeview High School, we tested a ban for one full school year. Each morning, students placed their phones in locked pouches that opened only at dismissal. We then compared that year with the year before. Office referrals for classroom disruptions dropped from 412 to 236. Teachers reported that phone-related problems, such as students recording fights, posting photos of classmates without permission, and texting answers during tests, nearly disappeared. In an anonymous survey, 81 percent of our teachers said students were more focused during lessons.

Students noticed the difference, too. Our librarian reported that lunch-period visits to the library more than doubled. A cafeteria that had been strangely quiet, with students staring at screens, became loud with conversation. Several students told me they felt relieved not to worry all day about what was being posted about them.

The benefits go beyond grades and behavior. A growing number of researchers have raised concerns about links between heavy social media use and anxiety, poor sleep, and loneliness among teenagers. A school day without phones gives young people several hours each day to practice paying attention and talking face to face.

Some parents worry about emergencies. I understand that concern; I am a parent, too. But during an emergency, students need to listen to adults and follow instructions, not scroll through rumors or tie up phone lines with calls. Parents can always reach their children by calling the front office, just as families did for generations.

I will be honest: one school's experience does not prove that a ban will work everywhere, and our results come from a single year. But the evidence we have points in one direction. When phones are put away, students pay attention, conflicts decline, and classrooms become places for learning again. High schools should give every student that chance.

stimuli.title: Teach Responsibility Instead of Banning Phones
stimuli.source: By Denise Harmon, parent of two high school students. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
When my daughter's high school was evacuated last fall because of a gas leak, the first news I received came from her: a text message that said, “We're OK, outside on the football field.” The school's official announcement arrived forty minutes later. I will never forget that feeling of relief. A total cell phone ban would take that connection away from every family.

Supporters of phone bans talk as if phones were nothing but toys. In reality, phones are tools. Students use them to photograph notes on the board, to check due dates in online classroom systems, and to look up words they do not understand. For students who are still learning English, a translation app can be the difference between following a lesson and sitting lost. Banning phones outright throws away these benefits along with the distractions.

Bans also cost money and time. Locking pouches can cost about $30 each. For a school of 1,200 students, that is $36,000, money that could pay for tutoring or new books. And someone has to enforce the rule. Teachers tell me they already have too little time to teach; under a ban, they will spend part of every class checking whether pouches are sealed.

Most important, a ban does not teach students anything. In a few short years, these young people will be in workplaces and college classrooms where no one locks away their phones. They need to learn self-control now, while adults are around to guide them. Every parent I know agrees that responsibility is learned through practice, not prohibition.

There is a better way. Schools can require phones to be silenced and put away during class while allowing students to use them between classes and at lunch. Teachers can invite students to use phones for specific learning tasks. Students who break the rules can lose their phone privileges for a set period. This approach targets the real problem, distraction during lessons, without cutting students off from their families or from useful tools.

Phones are a permanent part of modern life. Instead of pretending otherwise, our high schools should teach students how to use them wisely.

stimuli.title: Engines of Wind and Water: How Hurricanes Form
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Every year from June through November, forecasters who watch the Atlantic Ocean pay close attention to the tropics. Somewhere over warm water, a cluster of thunderstorms may begin to spin. Most of these clusters fade within a day or two. A few, however, grow into hurricanes, which are among the most powerful storms on Earth.

[2] A hurricane works like a giant heat engine, and its fuel is warm, moist air rising from the ocean. When the sun heats tropical seas, water evaporates into the air above. As this moist air rises, it cools, and the water vapor condenses into the tiny droplets that form clouds. Condensation releases heat, the same energy that was absorbed when the water evaporated. That released heat warms the surrounding air, making it lighter, so it rises even faster. As air rushes upward, the air pressure at the ocean's surface drops, and more warm, moist air flows in to replace the rising air. As long as the storm stays over warm water, this cycle feeds itself.

[3] Several conditions must come together for a hurricane to form. The ocean surface usually must be at least 80 degrees Fahrenheit (about 27 degrees Celsius), and the warm layer must extend to a depth of roughly 150 feet. The air must be moist, so that rising air keeps producing clouds. Winds at different heights must also blow at similar speeds and from similar directions. When winds high in the atmosphere are much stronger than those near the surface, a condition called wind shear, they tear the top of a developing storm away from its base, and the storm falls apart.

[4] Finally, the storm needs to spin. Because Earth rotates, winds that travel long distances curve, bending to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. This bending, called the Coriolis effect, sets storms rotating; hurricanes north of the equator turn counterclockwise. The Coriolis effect is weakest near the equator, which is why hurricanes almost never form within a few hundred miles of it, even though the water there is plenty warm.

[5] Forecasters track a developing storm through a series of stages. A cluster of thunderstorms that holds together for a day or more is called a tropical disturbance. When its winds begin circling a clear center at sustained speeds of up to 38 miles per hour, it becomes a tropical depression. At 39 miles per hour, it becomes a tropical storm and receives a name. At 74 miles per hour, it is officially a hurricane. A mature hurricane has a calm, often clear center called the eye, surrounded by a towering ring of thunderstorms called the eyewall, where the strongest winds blow.

[6] A hurricane begins to weaken when it loses its fuel. Moving over cooler water or over land cuts off its supply of warm, moist air. But a weakening storm can still be deadly. Although hurricanes are ranked by wind speed, water usually causes the most harm. Storm surge, a dome of seawater pushed ashore by the storm's winds, has historically been the leading cause of hurricane deaths in the United States. Heavy rain can also flood communities hundreds of miles inland, long after the winds have died down.

[7] Scientists cannot prevent hurricanes, but they have become far better at predicting where storms will go. Thanks to weather satellites, aircraft that fly directly into storms, and powerful computer models, forecasts of a hurricane's path are much more accurate today than they were a few decades ago. That extra warning gives families time to do the thing that saves the most lives: get out of the way.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Although many people doubted it, the Erie Canal overcame great engineering challenges and transformed trade and growth in New York and the West, even though not everyone benefited.
The Erie Canal failed to earn back its cost because railroads replaced it within a few years of its opening.
Thomas Jefferson's refusal to fund the Erie Canal shows that the federal government opposed the settlement of the West.
The most important part of the Erie Canal's story is Canvass White's invention of a cement that hardened underwater.
items.explain:
The passage moves from the problem the canal was meant to solve (paragraph 1), through the doubts it faced (paragraph 2) and how it was built (paragraphs 3–4), to its effects (paragraph 5) and its costs and legacy (paragraph 6). Only the statement that the canal overcame doubts and engineering challenges, transformed trade and growth, and did not benefit everyone captures all of this.

The canal did earn back its cost: tolls “repaid the state's roughly $7 million construction cost within about ten years” (paragraph 5), and railroads took freight only “within a few decades.” Jefferson's comment and White's cement are single details, not the central idea.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 2.

“President Thomas Jefferson reportedly dismissed the plan as ‘little short of madness.’”

As used in the sentence, what does dismissed mean?
options: removed from a job
delayed until a later time
rejected as not worth serious thought
studied carefully before deciding
items.explain:
Calling a plan “little short of madness” means treating it as foolish. In this context, dismissed means rejected as not worth serious thought.

“Removed from a job” is another meaning of dismissed, but a plan cannot be fired. Nothing suggests Jefferson delayed the plan or studied it carefully; his comment shows the opposite.

items.prompt: Paragraph 5 is shown below. Click the sentence that best supports the claim that building the canal was a sound use of the state's money.
spans: To celebrate, Governor Clinton traveled by boat from Buffalo to New York City, where he poured a keg of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean in a ceremony called the “Wedding of the Waters.”
The results soon silenced most critics.
The cost of shipping a ton of goods between Buffalo and New York City fell from about $100 to about $10, and goods moved far faster than they ever had by wagon.
Tolls collected from canal boats repaid the state's roughly $7 million construction cost within about ten years.
New York City became the busiest port in the nation, and towns along the route, such as Syracuse, Rochester, and Buffalo, grew into cities.
Thousands of settlers rode the canal west to Ohio, Michigan, and beyond.
items.explain:
The sentence “Tolls collected from canal boats repaid the state's roughly $7 million construction cost within about ten years” shows that the state got its money back, which directly supports the claim that the canal was a sound investment for the state.

The sentence about shipping costs shows that the canal helped shippers and farmers, but it does not show whether the state recovered what it spent.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 1, which conclusion can be drawn about western farmers before the Erie Canal was built?
options: They refused to sell their crops to buyers in East Coast cities.
They grew flour as their only crop.
They paid for the first roads across the Appalachian Mountains.
Much of their trade flowed south toward New Orleans rather than east toward New York.
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 says that “many western farmers found it cheaper to float their crops down the Mississippi River to New Orleans than to send them east.” So much of their trade went south, which explains why New York leaders saw “an opportunity.”

The passage never says farmers refused eastern buyers; the problem was cost, not refusal. Flour is one example of a load, not the only crop, and nothing is said about who paid for mountain roads.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, in what order did these events happen? Drag each event into the correct position.
choices: New York decides to build the canal without federal money.
Supporters ask the federal government to help pay for a canal.
Governor Clinton pours Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean.
Digging begins in Rome, New York.
items.explain: (1) In 1809, supporters asked the federal government for help (paragraph 2). (2) “Turned down by Washington, New York decided to build the canal on its own” (paragraph 2). (3) Construction began on July 4, 1817, in Rome (paragraph 3). (4) After the canal opened in October 1825, Clinton held the “Wedding of the Waters” (paragraph 5).

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 4?
options: to argue that the locks cost more than the rest of the canal
to explain how builders overcame the difference in height between Lake Erie and the Hudson River
to describe the working conditions of the immigrant laborers
to compare the Erie Canal with the railroads that replaced it
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 opens by naming the challenge (Lake Erie is about 570 feet higher than the Hudson, and “boats cannot float uphill”) and then explains the solution: 83 locks, including the staircase of locks at Lockport.

The paragraph says nothing about what the locks cost, how laborers lived (paragraph 3 mentions the workers), or railroads (paragraph 6).

items.prompt: Which details from the passage best support the claim that the Erie Canal changed the flow of trade in ways that benefited New York City? Select two answers.
options: New York City became the busiest port in the nation.
The cost of shipping a ton of goods between Buffalo and New York City fell from about $100 to about $10.
The finished canal was 40 feet wide and only 4 feet deep.
Clinton's opponents warned that the project would bankrupt the state.
Canvass White developed a cement that hardened underwater.
Visitors came from far away to watch boats rise at Lockport.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 reports that shipping costs between Buffalo and New York City fell by about 90 percent and that New York City “became the busiest port in the nation.” Together these show that goods now flowed cheaply to New York City instead of south to New Orleans.

The canal's size, White's cement, and the Lockport visitors describe how the canal was built or viewed, not its effect on trade. The opponents' warning was a prediction that turned out to be wrong.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, why does the author compare a lock to “a water elevator”?
options: to suggest that the locks were powered by motors like modern elevators
to help readers picture how a lock raises or lowers a boat from one level to another
to warn readers that the locks were dangerous to use
to show that the canal was more modern than the railroads
items.explain:
An elevator moves people between floors; a lock moves boats between water levels. The comparison helps readers picture the process the author then describes: a boat enters a chamber and “rises or falls to the next level” as water is let in or drained out.

The comparison is about what a lock does, not what powers it. The passage says the locks worked by letting water in or out, not by motors.

items.prompt: Overall, how does the author of “Clinton's Ditch” seem to judge the Erie Canal?
options: It was a costly mistake that harmed more people than it helped.
It mattered mainly because it later became a place for boating and cycling.
It succeeded only because the federal government eventually paid for it.
It was a remarkable achievement whose benefits were real but not shared by everyone.
items.explain:
The author praises the canal's success (“The results soon silenced most critics”; it “proved that a bold public project … could reshape the economy of an entire region”) but also notes in paragraph 6 that “Not everyone gained,” pointing to the loss of Native lands.

The author does not call the canal a mistake. Today's recreation is mentioned only at the end. New York built the canal “on its own,” so the federal government did not pay for it.

items.prompt: A reader argues that Jefferson's doubts about the canal were understandable in 1809, even though the canal later succeeded. Which detail from the passage best supports this reader's argument?
options: Tolls repaid the canal's construction cost within about ten years.
New York City became the busiest port in the nation.
The proposed canal would run about 363 miles, but the longest canal in the United States at the time ran only about 27 miles.
Visitors came from far away to watch boats rise at Lockport.
items.explain:
The reader's claim is about what was known in 1809. At that time, no American canal was longer than about 27 miles, and the proposed canal would be more than thirteen times as long (363 ÷ 27 ≈ 13.4), through “forests, swamps, and rocky ridges.” That makes doubt reasonable before the canal was built.

The tolls and New York City's growth happened after the canal opened, so they show that the doubts turned out to be wrong, not that they were understandable. The Lockport visitors do not relate to Jefferson's doubts.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I was sorry to learn that your new dining table arrived nine days late and that one of {{0}} legs was cracked.”

options: it's
its
its'
their

items.explain:
The legs belong to the table, so the sentence needs the possessive pronoun its, which never takes an apostrophe.

“It's” means “it is” (“one of it is legs” makes no sense). “Its'” is not a word. “Their” is plural and does not match the singular “table.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Unfortunately, a winter storm delayed the delivery truck, and the box was damaged when it {{0}} from one truck to another at our regional center.”

options: is moved
was moved
will be moved
moves

items.explain:
The damage happened in the past (“the box was damaged”), so the clause that tells when it happened also needs the past tense: was moved.

“Is moved” and “moves” are present tense, and “will be moved” is future; none of them fit an event that has already happened.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The quality of our furniture and the satisfaction of our customers {{0}} our top priorities, and we fell short of both.”

options: is
are
was
has been

items.explain:
The subject is compound: “The quality … and the satisfaction.” Two subjects joined by and are plural and need a plural verb: are. The plural noun “priorities” confirms this.

“Is,” “was,” and “has been” are singular. Writers often choose them because the nearby words “furniture” and “customers” hide the real subject.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“We have already shipped a replacement table{{0}} should arrive by Friday, March 14.”

options: , it
it
; it
, it then

items.explain:
“We have already shipped a replacement table” and “it should arrive by Friday, March 14” are both independent clauses. A semicolon can correctly join two independent clauses: “…a replacement table; it should arrive….”

A comma alone (“, it” or “, it then”) creates a comma splice, and no punctuation at all (“ it”) creates a fused sentence.

items.prompt:
In the letter, the opening phrase below needs to describe the right noun.

“Packed in a reinforced wooden crate, {{0}}.”

Which option completes the sentence correctly?

options: you should receive the replacement table in perfect condition
our drivers will deliver the replacement table in perfect condition
the replacement table should arrive in perfect condition
we expect the replacement table to arrive in perfect condition

items.explain:
An introductory modifier describes the noun that comes right after the comma. The thing “packed in a reinforced wooden crate” is the table, so the sentence must continue with the replacement table.

The other choices place “you,” “our drivers,” or “we” after the comma, which would mean that the customer, the drivers, or the company was packed in the crate. These are dangling modifiers.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}}, you do not need to repack it or return it yourself.”

options: However
For example
Therefore
Similarly

items.explain:
The previous sentence says the driver will take the damaged table away. Not needing to return it yourself is a result of that, so the cause-and-effect transition Therefore is correct.

“However” signals a contrast, “For example” introduces an example, and “Similarly” signals a comparison; none of these relationships fits.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Please {{0}} our sincere apology, along with a $50 credit that has been added to your account.”

options: except
accept
expect
excepted

items.explain:
Accept means “to receive or agree to take,” which is what the writer is asking the customer to do with the apology.

“Except” means “other than” or “to leave out,” and “excepted” is its past form. “Expect” means “to anticipate,” which does not make sense in a request.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“If you have any other questions, please call my assistant or {{0}} at 555-0142.”

options: I
me
myself
mine

items.explain:
The pronoun is an object of the verb “call,” so it must be in the objective case: me. A quick test is to remove “my assistant or”: “please call me,” not “please call I.”

“Myself” is a reflexive pronoun and should be used only when the subject of the sentence is also “I.” “Mine” is possessive and does not fit.

items.prompt: What do the details in paragraph 2, “He meant to work quickly” and the trash bags and single box he brought, suggest about Theo at the beginning of the story?
options: He has already decided to keep most of his grandfather's tools.
He plans to treat clearing the workshop as a chore to get through rather than a chance to remember his grandfather.
He is worried that his mother will criticize the way he sorts the tools.
He intends to finish the rocking chair before the house is sold.
items.explain:
Theo brings “a roll of trash bags” and only “one cardboard box for anything worth selling,” and he “meant to work quickly.” He expects to throw most things away and leave, which shows he sees the job as a chore.

Nothing suggests he planned to keep the tools or that his mother would criticize him. He does not even know the chair is meant for him until paragraph 4, so he could not have planned to finish it.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the author writes that the rocking chair was “standing in the middle of the floor like a guest who had arrived too early.” What is the effect of this simile?
options: It makes the unfinished chair seem almost alive, as if it is waiting for something and cannot be ignored.
It shows that the chair is too large for the workshop.
It suggests that the chair belongs to a visitor rather than to the family.
It reveals that Theo is angry that someone left the chair in his way.
items.explain:
A guest who arrives too early is present before things are ready, and the host must deal with them. Comparing the unfinished chair to such a guest makes it seem like a living presence that is waiting, one Theo cannot simply walk past.

The simile is about timing and presence, not size or ownership, and nothing in the paragraph shows Theo is angry.

items.prompt: Paragraph 7 is shown below. Click the sentence in which Theo does what his grandfather once told him to do.
spans: His first stroke skipped and chattered across the wood.
His second tore a small chip from the edge, and he muttered under his breath.
He set the plane down and studied the board, following the fine lines that ran through it like currents in a slow river, and then he turned it around.
This time, the blade slid forward, and a thin, curling ribbon of cedar rose from it and dropped to the floor.
items.explain:
In paragraph 3, Grandpa Elias told Theo, “Don't fight the wood. Read the grain. It will tell you which way it wants to go.” In the third sentence of paragraph 7, Theo stops, studies “the fine lines that ran through it,” which are the grain, and turns the board to work in the direction the grain runs.

The last sentence shows the result of following the advice (the blade finally slides smoothly), but the action of reading the grain happens in the third sentence. The first two sentences show Theo fighting the wood, just as he did at twelve.

items.prompt: In paragraph 6, Theo tests the blade and finds it sharp. What does the narrator's comment “Of course it was” suggest?
options: Theo is surprised that the blade still works after months without use.
Theo is afraid he will cut himself on the blade.
Theo realizes that his grandfather always kept his tools carefully cared for and ready to use.
Theo suspects that his mother sharpened the blade before he arrived.
items.explain:
“Of course it was” shows that the sharp blade is exactly what Theo should have expected. It fits what he knows about his grandfather, whom he had seen test a blade “a hundred times” and who kept the plane “in its place on the pegboard.”

“Of course” signals the opposite of surprise. Nothing suggests fear or that his mother had been in the workshop.

items.prompt: Which details show that Theo's attitude toward the job of clearing out the workshop changes over the course of the story? Select two answers.
options: the trash bags still folded on the workbench at the end of the week
Theo's answer of “Slowly” when his mother asks how the clearing out is going
the smell of cedar shavings and machine oil in the workshop
the funeral that took place in March
a neighbor's lawn mower droning and stopping outside
the pencil marks on the unfinished rocker
items.explain:
Theo “meant to work quickly” and brought trash bags to clear the workshop. By the end, he tells his mother the work is going “Slowly,” and the trash bags are “still folded on the workbench.” Both details show that he has stopped clearing out the workshop and is working on the chair instead.

The smell, the funeral, the lawn mower, and the pencil marks are setting or background details. They do not show a change in Theo.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Young people should always do what their elders tell them.
Selling a family home is the hardest part of losing a loved one.
Skill with tools comes naturally to people with talent.
Honoring someone we have lost can mean patiently carrying on the work they began.
items.explain:
Theo finds the chair his grandfather was building for him and, instead of clearing the workshop, begins to finish it, slowly learning to “read the grain” as his grandfather taught. The story suggests that continuing a loved one's work is a way of honoring and staying connected to them.

The story does not teach blind obedience; Theo's change is his own choice. The house sale is only background. Theo's first strokes fail, so the story shows skill being learned with patience, not coming naturally.

items.prompt: How does paragraph 3 contribute to the story as a whole?
options: It shows that Theo has been an expert woodworker since he was a child.
It provides a memory that explains the grandfather's advice and Theo's earlier refusal to learn, which gives meaning to his later choice to pick up the plane.
It explains why Theo's mother has decided to sell the house.
It introduces a conflict between Theo and his mother that is resolved at the end.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 is a flashback. It shows twelve-year-old Theo giving up after one mistake and records the advice “Read the grain.” Without this memory, readers would not understand why Theo studies the grain in paragraph 7 or why his choice to keep working matters.

The flashback shows Theo was not skilled; he tore the board and quit. It says nothing about the house sale, and the story never presents a conflict between Theo and his mother.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a high school principal who supports banning student cell phones during the school day and a parent who opposes such a ban.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The annual spring cleanup of {{0}} will take place on Saturday, April 19, from 8:00 a.m. to noon.”

options: riverside park
Riverside park
Riverside Park
riverside Park

items.explain:
Riverside Park is the name of a specific place, so it is a proper noun, and every main word in it is capitalized, including “Park.”

A common noun such as “a park” is lowercase, but when “park” is part of a name, it is capitalized.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Last year, more than sixty volunteers {{0}} over 1,200 pounds of trash from the park and the riverbank.”

options: collect
will collect
collected
are collecting

items.explain:
“Last year” places the action in the past, so the sentence needs the simple past tense: collected.

“Collect” and “are collecting” are present tense, and “will collect” is future; none of them fit an action that happened last year.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“…and the committee expects this year's turnout to be even larger {{0}} last year's.”

options: then
than
as
from

items.explain:
Than is used to make comparisons (“larger than last year's”).

Then refers to time (“first this, then that”), so it is a common but incorrect choice here. “Larger as” and “larger from” are not standard ways to make a comparison.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“They will plant native wildflowers near the playground, repaint the picnic benches, and {{0}}.”

options: repairing the trail signs
the trail signs will be repaired
to be repairing the trail signs
repair the trail signs

items.explain:
Items in a series should have the same grammatical form. The first two items are base verbs following “will”: “plant … , repaint … , and repair the trail signs.”

“Repairing” switches to an -ing form, “the trail signs will be repaired” switches to a full clause in the passive voice, and “to be repairing” is awkward and does not match the other verbs.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Because the work will be spread across several areas of the park{{0}} of all ages and abilities are needed.”

options: . Volunteers
, volunteers
; volunteers
, and volunteers

items.explain:
“Because the work will be spread across several areas of the park” is a dependent clause; it cannot stand alone. When a dependent clause begins a sentence, it is joined to the main clause with a comma: “…of the park, volunteers of all ages and abilities are needed.”

A period would leave the “Because” clause as a fragment. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and adding “and” after a “because” clause breaks the sentence's logic.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Children under 14 are welcome, but {{0}} parents or guardians must sign a permission form before the event.”

options: there
they're
their
theirs

items.explain:
The parents belong to the children, so the sentence needs the possessive pronoun their.

“There” refers to a place, “they're” means “they are,” and “theirs” is a possessive pronoun that stands alone (“the forms are theirs”) and cannot come before a noun.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Anyone {{0}} schedule does not allow a full morning can still help for an hour or two.”

options: who's
whose
who
whom

items.explain:
The schedule belongs to “anyone,” so the sentence needs the possessive whose.

“Who's” means “who is” (“anyone who is schedule” makes no sense). “Who” and “whom” are not possessive and cannot come directly before “schedule” here.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the article. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}}, late registrants are still welcome to join.”

options: However
Therefore
For example
Similarly

items.explain:
The previous sentence offers a free T-shirt to volunteers who register by April 12. This sentence adds that people who register late can still take part, which is a contrast with the deadline. However signals that contrast.

“Therefore” would wrongly suggest that late registrants are welcome because of the T-shirt offer. “For example” and “Similarly” do not fit the relationship between the sentences.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: A hurricane's winds are the most dangerous part of the storm.
Hurricanes form most often near the equator, where ocean water is warmest.
Hurricanes form and grow when warm water, moist air, steady winds, and Earth's rotation work together, and understanding them helps people prepare.
Satellites and computer models have made hurricanes weaker than they were in the past.
items.explain:
Paragraphs 2–5 explain how a hurricane draws energy from warm, moist air and what conditions it needs; paragraphs 6–7 explain how it weakens, why it is dangerous, and how forecasting helps people get out of the way.

Paragraph 6 says that water, not wind, “usually causes the most harm.” Paragraph 4 says hurricanes “almost never form” near the equator. Forecasting improves predictions; it does not weaken storms.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, why does the author describe a hurricane as working “like a giant heat engine”?
options: to show that, like an engine burning fuel, a hurricane runs on energy from warm, moist air and keeps going as long as that supply lasts
to suggest that hurricanes are caused by heat from factories and machines
to explain that hurricanes make the ocean much hotter than it was before
to show that hurricanes always travel at a steady speed
items.explain:
The author says the hurricane's “fuel is warm, moist air” and that the cycle continues “as long as the storm stays over warm water.” An engine runs while it has fuel, so the comparison explains where a hurricane gets its energy and why it keeps going.

The passage never mentions factories, says nothing about the storm heating the ocean, and does not discuss the speed at which hurricanes travel.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, sort each condition by its likely effect on a tropical storm system. Drag each condition into the correct box.
choices: The ocean surface beneath the storm is 84°F.
Winds high in the atmosphere are much stronger than winds near the surface.
Moist air rises steadily from the sea.
The storm system sits about 50 miles from the equator.
Water vapor condenses and releases heat.
bins: Helps the storm form or strengthen
Prevents the storm from forming or weakens it
items.explain:
Helps: Water of at least 80°F (paragraph 3), moist rising air (paragraphs 2–3), and the heat released by condensation (paragraph 2) all feed the storm.

Prevents or weakens: Strong winds aloft are wind shear, which tears a storm apart (paragraph 3). Moving over land cuts off the supply of warm, moist air (paragraph 6). Near the equator, the Coriolis effect is too weak to start the storm spinning (paragraph 4).

items.prompt: A cluster of thunderstorms is sitting over 85°F ocean water about 50 miles north of the equator. Based on the passage, why is it unlikely to become a hurricane?
options: The water is too cool to supply the storm with energy.
The air near the equator is always too dry to form clouds.
Storms near the equator always turn clockwise.
The Coriolis effect is too weak there to start the storm spinning.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 says, “The Coriolis effect is weakest near the equator, which is why hurricanes almost never form within a few hundred miles of it, even though the water there is plenty warm.” Fifty miles is well within that zone.

85°F is above the 80°F the passage gives as the usual minimum, so the water is warm enough. The passage does not say equatorial air is dry, and it says Northern Hemisphere hurricanes turn counterclockwise.

items.prompt: Paragraph 6 is shown below. Click the sentence that directly contrasts the way hurricanes are ranked with the thing that makes them most harmful.
spans: A hurricane begins to weaken when it loses its fuel.
Moving over cooler water or over land cuts off its supply of warm, moist air.
But a weakening storm can still be deadly.
Although hurricanes are ranked by wind speed, water usually causes the most harm.
Storm surge, a dome of seawater pushed ashore by the storm's winds, has historically been the leading cause of hurricane deaths in the United States.
Heavy rain can also flood communities hundreds of miles inland, long after the winds have died down.
items.explain:
“Although hurricanes are ranked by wind speed, water usually causes the most harm” sets up the contrast in one sentence: storms are ranked by wind, but water does the most harm.

The next two sentences give examples of the harm water causes (storm surge and inland flooding), but they do not mention how hurricanes are ranked.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what happens right after water vapor in rising air condenses into cloud droplets?
options: The sun heats the surface of the tropical sea.
Heat is released, warming the surrounding air so that it rises even faster.
The air pressure at the ocean's surface rises.
The cooled air sinks back down to the ocean.
items.explain:
Paragraph 2 explains: “Condensation releases heat…. That released heat warms the surrounding air, making it lighter, so it rises even faster.”

The sun heating the sea happens earlier in the cycle. The passage says surface pressure drops, not rises, and it never describes air sinking back to the ocean.

items.prompt: A storm system over the ocean has a clear center and sustained winds of 55 miles per hour. Based on paragraph 5, which statements are true about this storm? Select two answers.
options: It is classified as a tropical storm.
It has been given a name.
It is classified as a tropical depression.
It is officially a hurricane.
It has stopped drawing energy from the ocean.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 says a system becomes a tropical storm “at 39 miles per hour” and “receives a name” at that stage. It does not become a hurricane until 74 miles per hour. Since 39 ≤ 55 < 74, the storm is a named tropical storm.

A tropical depression has winds of up to 38 miles per hour, so 55 is too fast. A storm still over warm ocean water keeps drawing energy from it.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the passage is organized?
options: It explains a natural process, how a hurricane forms, grows, and weakens, and then describes how people respond to the danger.
It tells the history of famous hurricanes in the order in which they struck.
It compares Atlantic hurricanes with storms in the Southern Hemisphere.
It describes a problem and argues that scientists should find a way to stop hurricanes from forming.
items.explain:
The passage moves through the hurricane's life: its energy source (paragraph 2), the conditions it needs (paragraphs 3–4), its stages (paragraph 5), and its weakening and dangers (paragraph 6). It ends with forecasting and evacuation (paragraph 7).

No specific historical storms are described. The Southern Hemisphere is mentioned only once. The author states that “scientists cannot prevent hurricanes” and does not argue that they should.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 7?
options: to argue that aircraft should no longer fly into hurricanes
to show that hurricanes have become less common in recent decades
to explain why better forecasting matters even though hurricanes cannot be prevented
to describe the parts of a mature hurricane
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 admits that “scientists cannot prevent hurricanes” and then explains that improved forecasts give families time to “get out of the way,” which the author calls “the thing that saves the most lives.”

The paragraph mentions aircraft as a forecasting tool, not something to stop. It says nothing about how common hurricanes are, and the parts of a hurricane (eye and eyewall) are described in paragraph 5.

items.prompt: Based on the graph and the table, on which day was Hurricane Marisa first measured at hurricane strength?
options: Day 2
Day 3
Day 4
Day 5
items.explain:
A storm is a hurricane at 74 mph or more. Marisa's measured winds were 45 mph on Day 2 and 70 mph on Day 3 (both tropical storm range, 39–73 mph), then 100 mph on Day 4. So Day 4 is the first day at hurricane strength.

Day 3 is a common error: 70 mph is close to 74 but still below the hurricane threshold.

items.prompt:
Use the graph and the table to complete the statement.

On Day 6, Marisa was a {{0}} hurricane. By Day 8, after two days over land, it had weakened to a {{1}}.

options: Category 2
Category 3
Category 4
Category 5
tropical depression
tropical storm
Category 1 hurricane

items.explain:
On Day 6, Marisa's winds were 135 mph. Since 130 ≤ 135 ≤ 156, it was a Category 4 hurricane.

On Day 8, its winds were 45 mph. Since 39 ≤ 45 ≤ 73, it had weakened to a tropical storm. It was not yet a tropical depression (38 mph or less).

items.prompt: Marisa's winds dropped from 135 mph on Day 6 to 90 mph on Day 7. Which explanation from the passage “Engines of Wind and Water” best accounts for this change?
options: Winds high in the atmosphere tore the top of the storm away from its base.
The Coriolis effect reversed the direction of the storm's spin.
Condensation in the eyewall released more heat than before.
Moving over land cut off the storm's supply of warm, moist air.
items.explain:
The data display states that Marisa “moved onto land early on Day 7.” Paragraph 6 of the passage explains that “moving over cooler water or over land cuts off its supply of warm, moist air,” which is the storm's fuel. That explains the sharp drop in wind speed (135 − 90 = 45 mph).

Wind shear can weaken a storm, but nothing in the data suggests it, while the landfall is stated directly. Condensation releasing heat would strengthen the storm, and the passage never says the Coriolis effect reverses.

items.prompt: A student looks at the graph and concludes: “By Day 8, Marisa's winds were only 45 mph, so the storm was no longer a serious danger to people.” Which information from the passage best challenges this conclusion?
options: A weakening storm can still be deadly, because heavy rain can flood communities hundreds of miles inland long after the winds have died down.
A tropical storm receives a name when its winds reach 39 miles per hour.
The ocean surface usually must be at least 80 degrees Fahrenheit for a hurricane to form.
Forecasts of a hurricane's path are more accurate today than they were a few decades ago.
items.explain:
The student judges danger by wind speed alone. Paragraph 6 warns that “a weakening storm can still be deadly” and that heavy rain can flood communities far inland “long after the winds have died down.” A 45-mph storm over land could still cause deadly flooding.

The naming rule, the water temperature needed for formation, and forecast accuracy are all true statements from the passage, but none of them addresses whether a weakened storm is still dangerous.
